subject: orthopaedics
title: Common Peroneal Nerve Injury

steps.tx: **Common peroneal nerve** is the most frequently injured major peripheral nerve of the lower extremity. Arising from the posterior divisions of the L4 to S2 spinal roots as the lateral division of the sciatic nerve, it descends through the popliteal fossa along the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon. It then winds anteriorly around the subcutaneous lateral neck of the fibula, where it is tightly bound to periosteum beneath the fibularis longus muscle.
steps.say: The common peroneal nerve originates from L4 through S2 roots. It winds tightly around the neck of the fibula right beneath the skin, where its superficial tethered course leaves it exceptionally vulnerable to trauma.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of peripheral nerve trunk and vulnerability points.
vis.caption: Anatomical course and superficial tethering points of the common peroneal nerve around the fibular neck. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Mechanism of injury** at the fibular neck commonly involves blunt trauma, lacerations, or traction stretching during knee dislocations. In severe knee dislocations with disruption of the posterolateral corner and fibular collateral ligament, traction forces tear the tethered common peroneal nerve in up to forty percent of cases. Iatrogenic injuries frequently occur from tight circumferential plaster casts, compression bandages, prolonged lithotomy surgical positioning, or retractor pressure during lateral high tibial osteotomy.
steps.say: Fibular neck trauma, direct lacerations, and knee dislocations frequently injure the nerve. Iatrogenic causes include tight plaster casts, pressure from surgical leg holders, and retractors during osteotomy.

left.title: Traumatic Traction Mechanisms
points: Disruption of posterolateral corner and FCL
Severe longitudinal traction neuropraxia or rupture

right.title: Compression / Iatrogenic Mechanisms
points: Tight plaster cast over fibular head
Prolonged lithotomy position in operating room
Habitual leg crossing in thin individuals
Primarily neurapraxia with high recovery rate

steps.tx: **Deep and superficial divisions** arise as the common peroneal nerve divides within the peroneus longus muscle belly. The deep peroneal nerve pierces the anterior intermuscular septum to innervate the anterior compartment muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and peroneus tertius, terminating as sensory innervation to the first dorsal web space. The superficial peroneal nerve courses through the lateral compartment, supplying peroneus longus and brevis and innervating dorsal foot skin.
steps.say: The nerve bifurcates into deep and superficial branches. The deep peroneal nerve drives ankle and toe dorsiflexion and senses the first web space, while the superficial branch powers foot eversion and senses the dorsal foot.

vis.title: Innervation Targets of Peroneal Nerve Branches
rows: Anterolateral distal leg and dorsal foot
Dorsum of foot and first web space combined
Entire plantar sole of the foot

steps.tx: **Foot drop** represents the cardinal motor presentation of common peroneal nerve palsy. Complete paralysis of the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus eliminates active ankle and toe dorsiflexion. Because the lateral evertors are also paralyzed, the unopposed action of the healthy tibialis posterior and gastrocnemius muscles pulls the foot into fixed equinovarus posture. During ambulation, the patient demonstrates a high-stepping equine gait to clear the toes off the floor.
steps.say: Foot drop is the hallmark motor sign: loss of active ankle dorsiflexion causes the toes to drag. To compensate and clear the floor during walking, the patient lifts the knee excessively high in a classic stepping gait.

steps.tx: **First dorsal web space** anesthesia constitutes the autonomous, pathognomonic sensory landmark of the deep peroneal nerve. In complete common peroneal palsy, sensory loss extends across the anterolateral lower leg and the entire dorsum of the foot. Crucially, the medial side of the foot and medial malleolus retain normal sensation supplied by the saphenous nerve (from the femoral nerve), while the lateral foot border is preserved by the sural nerve.
steps.say: The first dorsal web space between the big and second toes is the autonomous sensory zone of the deep peroneal nerve. In complete palsy, numbness covers the dorsal foot, but the medial ankle stays normal via the saphenous nerve.

right.title: Spared Cutaneous Territories

steps.tx: **Ankle-foot orthosis** (AFO) represents the mandatory immediate conservative intervention for acute foot drop. A lightweight thermoplastic posterior leaf-spring or carbon-fibre AFO maintains the foot in ninety degrees of neutral dorsiflexion during the swing phase of gait. This eliminates tripping, normalizes ground clearance, and prevents the development of fixed equinus contracture of the Achilles tendon while nerve regeneration proceeds. Daily passive stretching of the heel cord maintains ankle joint mobility.
steps.say: An ankle-foot orthosis holds the foot at ninety degrees, preventing the toes from dragging and stopping the Achilles tendon from tightening into a fixed contracture while awaiting nerve recovery.

vis.title: Conservative Management Protocol for Foot Drop
rows: Maintains ankle at 90 degrees in swing phase

steps.tx: **Electrodiagnostic studies** including nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography should be performed at three to four weeks post-injury. Testing at three weeks allows time for Wallerian degeneration to establish. Stimulating across the fibular neck differentiates local demyelinating conduction block (neurapraxia) with normal distal responses from axonal transection (axonotmesis or neurotmesis) characterized by absent motor responses and abundant fibrillation potentials.
steps.say: Order nerve conduction and electromyography studies at three to four weeks. This timing allows Wallerian degeneration to declare itself, separating simple neurapraxia from complete axonal rupture.

steps.tx: **Tibialis posterior tendon transfer** represents the definitive surgical salvage reconstruction for permanent, irreversible common peroneal nerve palsy failing to recover after twelve to eighteen months. The healthy, functioning tibialis posterior tendon is harvested from its navicular insertion, rerouted anteriorly through a generous window in the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula, and securely anchored into the lateral cuneiform or cuboid bone. This transfer successfully converts a deforming inverting force into an active dorsiflexor.
steps.say: When recovery fails after a year, transfer the tibialis posterior tendon through the interosseous membrane onto the lateral cuneiform. This converts an inverting force into an active foot dorsiflexor, liberating the patient from an orthosis.
